title: santa marta talks focused minds exit fossil fuels now hard part begins  ecmii 2026 05 13
text:
May 12 - The first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels has shifted the conversation from a narrow focus on emissions to transforming entire economies. But can the coalition of the willing who showed up at Santa Marta in Colombia last month become the coalition of the doing?
The 57 countries who took part in the summit, co-convened by Colombia and the Netherlands, together represent 30% of fossil supply and demand. “If you look at the Santa Marta group as potentially the largest clean-tech buyers’ group that has ever existed, here ​is a group saying, ‘we want to lead’,” says Nick Robins, senior director of finance and private sector at the WRI.
Now they must work out how. A science panel will help countries develop roadmaps for exiting fossil fuels, ‌and overcoming legal, financial and political barriers to transforming their economies. This work will link to countries’ national climate plans (Nationally Determined Contributions).
Colombia’s environment minister Irene Velez Torres said countries must be “very clear and honest” about emissions exported from producing countries. These are not usually counted in NDCs.
A draft roadmap for Colombia suggests that by 2050 emissions could be cut by 90% (compared with 2015) by 2050 through efficiency measures, renewables and storage, and widespread electrification.
The move away from fossil fuels will require an average extra $10 billion annual investment but could be delivering economy-wide savings of up to $23 billion a year by 2050.
Katrine Petersen, who works on clean ​power diplomacy at think-tank E3G, observes that the conference seems to have opened up conversations between importers and exporters – a recognition that “the transition away from something requires a transition to something”.
She adds: “You can’t leave countries to fend for themselves in trying ​to create pathways out of dependence, because so much of global trade is completely interconnected.”
Other outcomes of the conference include an agreement to hold a second conference next year, co-hosted by Ireland and ⁠Tuvalu, and workstreams to identify concrete opportunities in the energy transition.
Organisers won’t duplicate efforts by Brazil, president of last year’s COP climate talks in Belem, which committed to develop a global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels ahead of COP31, in Turkey, after 80 ​countries called for it.
Vicky Sins, who leads the climate and energy benchmark at the World Benchmarking Alliance (WBA), said the role of companies in the transition was also critical.
“You cannot have this dialogue without the private sector at the table to make sure that capital is being ​deployed to make the transition credible.” She adds that companies need to develop their own credible roadmaps, and be held accountable for delivering on them.
She says WBA will, alongside other coalitions, “mobilise the private sector to (look at) how do we align your capital, your production, your business models with the targets that you set?”
The WBA has just released its latest assessment of transition planning by financial institutions, and it finds that only two out of 400, ING and Zürcher Kantonalbank, have robust commitments to phase out fossil fuels.
WRI’s Robins senses a new phase in transition planning. “Companies and countries are now facing serious instability because of dependence on fossil fuels,” so it’s reasonable for investors to be asking about goals for reducing dependence. “Clean energy is now a stability investment,” he adds.
This raises a challenge for central banks, whose main job ​is to keep inflation under control. While interest rates are a key tool, raising them “could have unintended consequences on exactly the sectors you want to promote for stability, as well as climate reasons,” suggests Robins.
The conference heard from Ma Jun, a former chief economist at ​China central bank's research bureau about how it has advanced the country’s green financial system, including a decarbonisation facility charged at 1.25% interest, and by publishing a ranking of banks’ green loan ratios to create competition.
A working group of banks, researchers and policymakers has been formed to address financial stability challenges ‌posed by the ⁠transition, including the need for capacity-building in developing countries.
Champa Patel, executive director for governments and policy at international non-profit the Climate Group, says the collective group should “single-mindedly” focus on investment for emerging economies.
“A just transition isn't possible if countries have to absorb all the adjustment costs alone,” she says. “If we want a faster transition, then what's the role of concessional finance, private sector investments, blended finance?”
Some, including countries in the Global South which are emerging producers of oil and gas, “don't have access to the kind of capital they need for renewables expansion, for adaptation, and there's certainly not money on the table on the scale (needed) to forego oil and gas,” observes Valerie Marcel, co-founder of New Producers for Sustainable Energy.
This group of 22 countries provides peer to peer support to use resource development as a bridge to sustainability. One member, Senegal, ​is using its gas reserves to displace imports of heavy oil, ​freeing up capital to allocate to renewables.
Marcel’s group is helping ⁠member countries with capacity-building to put in place the regulations and monitoring to have near-zero methane oil and gas production. This will give them a competitive advantage, she says. “I don't think we should be purists about what the transition should look like in Global South countries.”
Fossil fuel subsidies and the high costs of capital are key roadblocks that need to be addressed. The former amounted to almost $1 trillion in ​2024. Now countries have a delicate balancing act to protect poorest citizens from the price hikes caused by the war with Iran, without further embedding subsidies.
As well as making subsidy inventories, participants ​at Santa Marta discussed how to ⁠create an enabling environment for international reform, with stronger carbon pricing and broader sectoral and geographic coverage. Over 50 countries already have carbon pricing schemes.
After the conference, the EU, Brazil and China launched a new coalition to support more effective and robust emissions trading systems that could help deliver more funds for decarbonisation, with New Zealand and Germany as its first members.
The private sector track advocated for subsidy reform, coupled with targeted cash transfers for vulnerable groups, and proactive use of public procurement to shift demand to renewables and electrification.
The Australian mining giant Fortescue, which co-led the private ⁠sector track in ​Colombia, is campaigning at home for a cap on diesel tax credits that it and other large miners receive.
In some areas, like shipping and aviation, global cooperation ​will be needed, but the conference urged countries to map their own fossil-fuel subsidies. This process is already under way in 17 countries, who formed a coalition at COP28.
Not all action has to happen at the national level. “We had 11 subnational governments who were talking about what they already do. Many of them have “polluter-pays” taxes, (and) powers ​to look at permitting (for) grid infrastructure,” observes Patel.
States such as California, Quebec and Hawaii are in the vanguard, able to showcase models that can be replicated or scaled, and identify gaps that national governments need to fill. “This level of government can actually help advance the agenda.”
This article has been updated to include new WBA data assessing financial institutions on planning for the energy transition.
